source_read: PDF, printed pp. 77–87 (all 11 pages; Tables 1, 2, 5, 6 and Figures 1–3 checked on pages rendered at 150 dpi; born-digital text layer agreed with the rendered pages)

claims.overstatement: None. The claim's 'cannot show recovery' matches the authors' own limitation (p. 86); their abstract and discussion present reversibility more hopefully, as possible.
claims.note: Numbers check: ex-ketamine group 344.43 (624.72) days since last use, range 120–2980; 2.55 (3.90) days a month just before stopping against the frequent group's current 20.13 (2.36); peak 11.21 (9.34) days a month. Two qualifiers the claim omits. (1) The ex-ketamine group was not uniformly lighter: 12 of 30 had been frequent and 8 daily, and it had the longest total use (7.63 years against 6.07 frequent and 4.20 infrequent), which the authors use to argue that less use does not explain the absence of deficits (p. 85). (2) Abstinence was self-reported; hair covering about the past 3 months gave a non-zero mean ketamine level in this group (3.55, SD 13.63 ng/mm), although the shortest reported abstinence was 120 days and no ketamine was found in either control group; the paper does not comment.

anchors.locator: Results › Neurocognitive assessments (SOC, PRM, source memory, prose recall, fluency paragraphs); Table 5 (p. 83); Abstract (p. 77)
anchors.extracted: Only the frequent group differed from others; ex-ketamine means at or above the control groups on every test (e.g. Stockings 8.89 vs 9.53 and 9.30; d' 2.97 vs 2.85 and 2.67; pattern recognition about 94.5% vs about 90% and 91% in Fig. 2; SWM errors about 11 vs about 19 and 16 in Fig. 1). Abstract: no differences between the infrequent or ex-ketamine groups and the other groups.

anchors.locator: Discussion › Limitations, 1st paragraph (with p. 85, Discussion › Neurocognitive function, 3rd paragraph)
anchors.extracted: Authors acknowledge that reversibility can only be shown by retesting the frequent group after a sufficient period of abstinence (p. 86); earlier (p. 85) they read the result as implying deficits may be reversible, arguing that 8 of the ex-ketamine group had used daily and the group had used longest.

claims.overstatement: Minor: 'at least 24 hours after any drug' should read 'after any psychotropic drug, by self-report': cigarettes were allowed during the session's breaks (p. 79), urine was analysed but no results are reported (p. 78), and the follow-up paper says 24-hour abstinence could not be verified biologically (Morgan et al., 2010b, p. 132). 'Reading-test estimate' is loose: Spot the Word is a lexical-decision (word versus non-word) vocabulary test. The claim correctly follows the results, not the abstract, which lists category fluency among the impairments although Results and Table 5 show no group difference.
claims.note: All numbers check. Figure readings (reader's): SWM errors about 32.4 (frequent) vs about 13.8, 11.2, 18.7 and 16.0 (Fig. 1, p. 82); pattern recognition about 83.3% vs about 91.7, 94.5, 90.3 and 91.1% (Fig. 2, p. 83), so 'about 32 against 11 to 19' and 'about 83% against 90% to 95%' are right. For SWM errors the text names no comparators (P < 0.01); 'compared to all other groups' is attached to the strategy score. Reader's Bonferroni recalculation from Table 5 (pooled variance, 10 pairs): Stockings lower than all four other groups (vs ex P about 0.035, not < 0.01); d' lower only than the ex group (P about 0.017; vs polydrug 0.11, vs infrequent 0.48, vs non-drug 1.0), the same as the editors' recalculation; SWM strategy not reproduced vs polydrug (P about 0.11). Education differed significantly only from the infrequent (P = 0.018) and non-drug (P = 0.04) groups, and Spot the Word only from the polydrug (P = 0.01) and infrequent (P = 0.04) groups (the non-drug group scored 47.13); the family-history test reproduces exactly (chi-square 12.59, P = 0.013). The same team's follow-up paper reports this same baseline session as 2 (SD 2.60) days since last use, range 1–14 (Morgan et al., 2010b, Table 2), against 1.6 (1.27), range 1–7 here.

anchors.locator: Method › Participants, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Procedure, 1st paragraph (continues on p. 79)
anchors.extracted: Five groups: frequent (more than 4 times a week), infrequent (less than 4 times a week but at least monthly), ex (abstinent at least 1 month), polydrug matched for other drugs, non-drug (no illicit drugs). Participants who used drugs to abstain from psychotropic drugs for at least 24 h before testing; urine analysed (results not reported); hair taken to verify group; 10-minute hourly breaks with cigarettes allowed.

anchors.locator: Results › Drug use data › Ketamine use, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Table 2 (p. 81)
anchors.extracted: 19 of 30 frequent participants reported daily use. Days since last use 1.6 (1.27), range 1–7 (frequent); 11.3 (9.36), range 1–28 (infrequent). Frequency 20.13 (2.36) vs 3.25 (2.55) days a month. Hair ketamine 282.14, 18.01 and 3.55 ng/mm in the three ketamine groups; none detected in either control group.

anchors.locator: Results › Correlations, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; p. 86 Discussion › Neurocognitive function, 5th paragraph, and Limitations, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: No covariate adjustment: one-way ANOVAs only. In the frequent group d' correlated with Spot the Word (r = 0.474, P = 0.009); education did not correlate with cognitive scores; self-reported amount did not correlate with any cognitive measure. Authors raise a withdrawal state as a possible cause of the frequent group's deficits (p. 86) and say pre-existing differences cannot be ruled out.

anchors.locator: Discussion › Neurocognitive function, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: Prose recall was unaffected, unlike the two earlier field studies; the authors suggest those deficits may reflect missed practice in designs that tested people first while intoxicated and again 3 days later; recreational use (about 3 days a month here) was not associated with impaired cognition.

anchors.locator: Abstract › Results and Conclusions
anchors.extracted: Abstract lists category fluency among the frequent group's impairments and speaks of episodic-memory impairment, while Results (p. 82) and Table 5 show no group difference in category fluency or prose recall; the Summary (p. 86) calls the impairments broad-ranging. An interpretation gap the claim avoids.

claims.overstatement: Minor: the general clause 'mostly below levels the authors regard as clinical' does not fit this study's depression result, whose frequent-group mean the authors place in the mild-to-moderate range (p. 85); the claim does report that label explicitly. Otherwise the wording stays at association.
claims.note: All values check against Table 6 (p. 84). Reader's Bonferroni recalculation from Table 6 (pooled variance, 10 pairs), the same as the editors': delusions inventory, frequent vs polydrug P about 0.008 and vs non-drug P about 0.0001 (vs infrequent 0.08 and ex 0.16, which the paper reports as P < 0.05); dissociation, frequent vs polydrug P about 0.014, vs non-drug and ex P < 0.001; depression only vs the ex group (P about 0.013; vs polydrug 0.11, non-drug 0.12, infrequent 1.0). Infrequent and ex groups' excess over the non-drug group on the delusions inventory, reported as P < 0.01: Bonferroni P about 0.48 and 0.27 (unadjusted 0.048 and 0.027). Infrequent vs non-drug on dissociation reproduces at about 0.009 (printed P < 0.001). The printed F values for the delusions inventory (8.40) and dissociation (6.60) are not reproduced from the table (about 5.9 and 8.3); both stay P < 0.001. r = 0.433, P = 0.019 fits n = 29.

anchors.extracted: Authors: pre-existing differences cannot be ruled out, though they read the amount-delusion correlation against that. Frequent group had more family history of mental illness (8 of 30 vs 1–3) and fewer years of education; childhood trauma, a risk factor for dissociation, was not assessed.

claims.overstatement: None; the claim labels the laboratory finding as second-hand.
claims.note: The laboratory statement is cited to Morgan et al. 2004 (Psychopharmacology 172: 298–308; reference 9 here), whereas Morgan et al. (2004a, Addiction, p. 1451) attributes the same finding (no residual effect 3 days later) to a different paper (Neuropsychopharmacology 29: 208–218), so which laboratory study shows it is unclear. Reference 9 is also cited on p. 85 for an opportunistic study of 18 people who used ketamine, which is the 2004 Addiction follow-up (reference 35): a citation error. The paper's description of Curran & Monaghan (2001) gives the less frequent group as using once a month.

anchors.locator: Introduction, 3rd paragraph
anchors.extracted: Second-hand: 3 days after a laboratory study, healthy volunteers who had received ketamine did not differ from those given placebo (ref. 9, Morgan et al. 2004, Psychopharmacology). Also describes Curran & Monaghan (2001): 18 frequent (about 13.5 days a month) vs 19 infrequent (once a month) participants equally impaired on the night; frequent group more impaired on episodic and semantic memory 3 days later.

anchors.locator: Discussion › Neurocognitive function, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: The same team's later reading: earlier day-3 prose-recall deficits may reflect missed practice in a design that tested people while intoxicated first and again 3 days later.

risk_of_bias.note: ROBINS-E high overall; confounding (education, premorbid estimate, family history, none adjusted) and selective reporting (abstract vs results, unreproducible post hoc tests) are the decisive domains.

interpretation_gap.note: Substantial: the abstract's category-fluency impairment, the 'delusional symptoms persist' conclusion and the reversibility inference all go beyond the printed results.

missed: Testing conditions (p. 78, Procedure, 1st paragraph, continuing on p. 79): cigarettes were allowed during hourly breaks, and the 24-hour abstinence from psychotropic drugs was self-reported; the follow-up paper says 24-hour abstinence could not be verified biologically for this same baseline session (Morgan et al., 2010b, p. 132).

Cross-paper: for this same baseline session, Morgan et al. (2010b, Table 2, p. 125) gives the frequent group's days since last use as 2 (SD 2.60), range 1-14 (here 1.6 (1.27), range 1-7), and its BDI for the 25 retested as 7.08 (here 11.48 for all 30, which would need a mean of about 33.5 in the 5 not retested). The 2010b card records the BDI and amount discrepancies; a cross-reference in RI 5 or the KF 1 note would help, since claims cite the 1-7 days and the 11.48 from this paper.

The laboratory statement on p. 78 (Introduction, 3rd paragraph), that volunteers given ketamine did not differ from placebo 3 days later, cites reference 9 (Psychopharmacology 2004; 172: 298-308), whereas Morgan et al. (2004a, Addiction, p. 1451) attributes the same finding to the Neuropsychopharmacology 2004 paper (29: 208-218); which laboratory study shows it is unclear. This matters for cl_ket_night_of_use_tests, which cites the finding second-hand from this paper.
